Lesson 01 / Text Editor GUI in Rust / build-first / ~60 minutes

Your Editor's First Window

Six stages, from an empty file to a window you can type code into — with the code folded away until you ask.

Your editor is a struct.
The GUI holds no state of its own — it draws that struct, and hands you a mutable borrow so you can change it.

How this variant works

This is lesson 1 turned inside out. The ordinary lesson shows you a change and then explains it. Here each stage gives you the brief first — what to build, where it goes, what it must do, and the words for the parts — and then gets out of the way, with the code folded up until you ask for it.

The honest problem with doing this in lesson 1 You cannot invent impl eframe::App for Editor on day one. Nobody can. A build-first lesson that pretends otherwise just wastes your afternoon. So every stage below is labelled with how much of it you could realistically derive, and the two stages that are pure transcription say so and give you a different job instead: name the parts, rather than guess them.

The three labels:

What the badge at the top of each stage means
transcription
Nobody derives this. Read the brief, look at the words, then open the fold and type it. Your job is to be able to point at each part and name it.
guided
You have seen every piece you need, but not in this arrangement. Attempt it. The hint names the idea you're missing; the fold has the answer.
yours
You have everything. Write it before you open anything. If you're stuck for ten minutes, take the hint — being stuck past that point stops teaching you.

Each stage runs: goal → what to build → what you'll need → how you'll know → folded hint → folded code → the words you just met. That last panel is the part to come back to. Lesson 1 throws about fifty new words at you and there is no way around that; what there is a way around is pretending you already know them.

Type it, don't paste it Your mission is to explain every line of this repo in an interview. Typing forces you to look at each token; pasting lets your eyes slide over it. Forty lines, about four minutes, the highest-leverage four minutes here. In this variant there is nothing to paste until you have already written your own anyway.

Before you start

rustc 1.97.1 via rustup, in ~/.cargo. If a terminal says "command not found: cargo", run source ~/.cargo/env.

The project is editor/, created with cargo new editor --bin and cargo add eframe — that put eframe = "0.36.1" in Cargo.toml and pulled 414 crates: windowing, GPU access, font shaping, clipboard. That's the work you are not doing.

Prove the toolchain works

The code is already written. Your job is to predict what it does before you run it.

Text appears in your terminal.

What to build

  1. Open editor/src/main.rs. cargo new already put three lines in it. Read them.
  2. Before running anything, say out loud — or write down — what each of the three lines does, and which of the two words on the middle line is not a normal function call. One of them has a mark on it that tells you it is something else.
  3. Then run it, from inside the editor directory.

What you'll need

cargo run does three things in a row: fetches and compiles your code and everything it depends on, links the result into a binary (a runnable file), and runs that binary. When people say "the toolchain works", this is the thing they just proved.

How you'll know

cd editor && cargo run
→ Hello, world!

Hint — what the punctuation is telling you

Two of the three lines are structure: something is being declared, and it has a body between braces. The name being declared is special — every Rust program starts there, and the compiler goes looking for that exact name.

On the middle line, look at the character immediately before the opening bracket. A normal function call does not have one. That mark means the thing in front of it is rewritten into other code before your program is compiled, which is how it can accept any number of arguments of any type — something a plain Rust function cannot do.

The code — it is already in your file; this is what it means

editor/src/main.rsthe whole file

fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}

fn declares a function; main is where every Rust program starts. println! ends in ! because it's a macro — rewritten into other code at compile time, which is how it takes any number of arguments of any type. The ! is always the tell.

Words you just met
crate
A Rust package — one library or one program. Your editor is a crate; so are the 414 things it depends on.
cargo
Rust's build tool and package manager. It fetches crates, compiles them, runs tests, and runs your program.
compile
Turn source text into machine code. Rust does this ahead of time, before the program runs — which is why the compiler can catch so much.
binary
The runnable file that comes out of compiling. --bin in cargo new said "this crate is a program, not a library".
function
A named block of code you can call. Declared with fn.
main
The function every Rust program starts at. Rename it and the program will not link.
macro
Code that writes code, expanded at compile time. Always called with a !, which is how you spot one at a glance.
argument
A value you pass into a call — "Hello, world!" here. The slot it lands in is a parameter.
token
The smallest piece of source the compiler reads as one unit: a name, a number, a bracket, an &. Half of this lesson is about single tokens.

An empty window

Four unfamiliar constructs at once, none derivable. Type it, then label it.

A blank 800×600 window opens on your desktop.

What to build

You are replacing the whole file with the smallest eframe application there is. It has four parts, and it is worth knowing what they are called before you look at them:

  1. A use declaration — one line that brings a name from another crate into scope so you can say egui instead of eframe::egui everywhere.
  2. A struct called Editor — a type you define. This one holds no data at all yet, which is honest: your editor knows nothing. This is your application. Not a window, not a widget — a plain data type you hang everything else off.
  3. An implementation of the trait eframe::App for that struct. A trait is a contract: a list of functions a type must provide in order to be usable somewhere. eframe::App is the contract for "something eframe can run", and it requires exactly one function, ui, which eframe calls to draw a frame. Leave its body empty — nothing drawn, blank window.
  4. A main that describes the window it wants and hands your type to eframe to run.

What you'll need

Deferred on purpose — we return in lesson 3 Everything inside main: NativeOptions, ..Default::default(), Box::new, and the |_cc| … closure. Four language features, none useful to you today, all interesting once you have ownership. Type it, run it, move on. You are not failing to understand it; you have not been taught it.

The one part worth staring at is the signature of ui. A signature is a function's name, its parameters and their types, and what it hands back. The trait fixes this one exactly — get it wrong and the compiler rejects the whole implementation, because you cannot half-implement a trait. It begins with &mut self, and stage 5 is entirely about that one token.

Two of the parameter names start with an underscore. That tells the compiler "I know I'm not using this, don't warn me." Drop the underscore on an unused variable and you get a warning — a small sample of how much Rust nags you, and how much of that nagging turns out to be useful.

How you'll know

cargo run
→ a blank window titled "editor"
First build takes ~30 seconds — it's compiling all 414 crates. Later builds are 1–2 seconds.

The code — open this one; there is nothing to derive

Replace the whole file. This is the smallest possible eframe application:

editor/src/main.rsreplacing the whole file

use eframe::egui;

struct Editor;

impl eframe::App for Editor {
    fn ui(&mut self, _ui: &mut egui::Ui, _frame: &mut eframe::Frame) {}
}

fn main() -> eframe::Result {
    let options = eframe::NativeOptions {
        viewport: egui::ViewportBuilder::default().with_inner_size([800.0, 600.0]),
        ..Default::default()
    };

    eframe::run_native("editor", options, Box::new(|_cc| Ok(Box::new(Editor))))
}

struct Editor; — a type holding no data at all. This is your application: not a window, not a widget, a plain data type you hang everything else off. Empty is honest — your editor knows nothing yet.

impl eframe::App for Editor — a trait implementation. A trait is a contract: functions a type must provide to be usable somewhere. eframe::App is the contract for "something eframe can run", and it requires one function, ui. Get the signature wrong and the compiler rejects it — you cannot half-implement a trait.

fn ui(&mut self, …) — what eframe calls to draw a frame. Empty body, nothing drawn, blank window. Note &mut self; stage 5 is entirely about that one token.

Your turn: label it

Transcription teaches nothing on its own, so do this before moving on. Looking only at what you typed, answer out loud:

  1. Which line is the trait implementation, and which two names does it join?
  2. How many parameters does ui take, and which one is not written with a type of its own?
  3. Which brackets in this file are a function body, and which are a struct's contents?
  4. eframe::run_native is handed three things. What is the first one, and where does it show up when you run the program?
The answers — check yourself, don't read first
  1. impl eframe::App for Editor — it joins the trait eframe::App to the type Editor. Read impl X for Y as "Y keeps X's promises".
  2. Three: &mut self, _ui, _frame. self is the one with no written type — it always means "the value this method was called on", so its type is already known.
  3. {} after the ui signature is an empty function body; the braces after impl … for Editor hold the implementation. struct Editor; has no braces at all — that is what a struct with no fields looks like.
  4. "editor", the window title. It is the text in the title bar of the window that just opened.
Words you just met
use declaration
A line that brings a name into scope, so you can write the short form. Not an #include — nothing is copied.
path (::)
How Rust spells "inside": eframe::egui is the egui name inside the eframe crate.
struct
A type you define by listing what it contains. A struct with nothing in it is written struct Editor; and is called a unit struct.
type
What a value is — String, Editor, f32. Rust checks every one of them before your program runs.
trait
A contract: the functions a type must provide to be usable somewhere. Other languages call the same idea an interface or a protocol.
implement (impl)
To provide those functions. impl Trait for Type is the whole grammar.
method
A function that belongs to a type and takes self — you call it as value.name().
signature
A function's name, parameters, their types, and its return type. A trait fixes the signature; you fill in the body.
parameter
A named slot in a function's signature. The value passed into it at a call site is the argument.
self
The value a method was called on. &mut self means "I may change it"; stage 5 is about why that matters.
reference (&)
A borrowed view of a value — access without ownership. The single most important symbol in Rust.
scope
The region of code where a name means something. Names go out of scope at the closing brace, and that is also when values get cleaned up.
return type
What a function hands back, written after ->. Here main returns eframe::Result — it can fail.
widget
One interactive thing on screen: a label, a button, a text box. In egui they do not survive between frames — see stage 6.

Draw something

The pieces are named for you; the arrangement is yours. Expect one compiler error.

The word "editor" appears in the window.

What to build

  1. Fill in the empty body of ui. Inside it, make a panel — a region of the window — and inside that, draw a heading reading editor.

What you'll need

Three names, which you could not have guessed and are not expected to:

  • egui::CentralPanel::default() makes the panel. CentralPanel takes whatever space other panels leave; later you'll add a top panel for tabs and a bottom one for a status bar, and this one shrinks around them automatically.
  • .show(ui, |ui| { … }) puts things in it. The second argument is a closure — an anonymous function written between the pipes. Read the whole call as "inside this panel, do the following".
  • ui.heading("editor") draws large text. Calls on the inner ui lay out top to bottom in the order you write them. There is no layout file and no positioning: the order of your statements is the layout.
You are meant to hit an error here — read it, don't skip it error[E0425]: cannot find value `ui` in this scope. Rust then spells out the fix: "the leading underscore in _ui marks it as unused, consider renaming it to ui." The underscore said "unused, don't warn me" — and now you are using it. Fix it yourself before reading further; this is the cheapest possible version of an error you will meet a hundred more times.

How you'll know

cargo run
→ the window now says editor in large text

Hint — how the three names fit together

They nest. The panel is built and immediately shown, in one chained expression; the closure you hand to .show is where the heading call goes. So the body of ui is one statement, and it ends in a semicolon.

Note that the closure's own parameter is also called ui. That is not a mistake — it is a fresh ui for the inside of the panel, and it shadows the outer one for the length of the closure. Inside the braces, ui means the panel's.

The code — open once yours draws, or once you're stuck

adding    removing    existing code, shown only for context

editor/src/main.rsin impl eframe::App for Editor

impl eframe::App for Editor {
    fn ui(&mut self, _ui: &mut egui::Ui, _frame: &mut eframe::Frame) {}
    fn ui(&mut self, ui: &mut egui::Ui, _frame: &mut eframe::Frame) {
        egui::CentralPanel::default().show(ui, |ui| {
            ui.heading("editor");
        });
    }
}

The red line and the green line differ by one character — the underscore on _ui. That is the whole of E0425.

Words you just met
panel
A region of the window. Panels claim space in the order they are added; CentralPanel takes what is left.
closure
An anonymous function written inline, its parameters between |pipes|. It can use names from around it, which is what makes it more than a function.
shadowing
Declaring a name that hides an outer one of the same name, for the length of a scope. Deliberate and common in Rust; not an error.
method chaining
Calling a method on the result of the last one: default().show(…). You will see long chains of these in egui.
expression
Anything that produces a value. Almost everything in Rust is one, which is why a whole panel can be built inside a single statement.
E0425
The compiler's numbered name for "cannot find this value". Every Rust error has a code, and rustc --explain E0425 prints an essay about it.

Give it something to remember

Three edits. One new trait, one new type distinction, and a second error you should hit on purpose.

A line of text you chose appears below the heading.

What to build

Three separate edits, in three parts of the file. Do them in order and don't run anything until all three are in — the file won't compile in between.

  1. An editor needs a buffer, so give Editor a field called text, of type String. Replace struct Editor; from stage 2 — don't add alongside it, or you define the same name twice. Then, just under it, implement the standard library's Default trait for Editor, so there is a sensible starting value: a function default() returning Self with text set to a line of your choosing.
  2. Draw that text. One line in fn ui, under the heading, using ui.label(…). Pass it a reference to your field, not the field itself.
  3. Elsewhere in the file: main no longer compiles. Fix it. Do this one by reading the error rather than by being told.

What you'll need

String vs &str. Rust has two string types and the difference matters constantly. A piece of text in quotes in your source — a string literal — is a &str: a borrowed view of text baked into the binary, fixed size, can't grow. A String is owned, lives on the heap, and can grow. A text buffer must grow, so the field is a String, and .to_owned() on a literal copies it into one.

.to_string(), .to_owned(), and String::from() are equivalent here. .to_owned() is the most precise about intent: I am taking ownership of a copy.

Self, with a capital S, is the type you are implementing on — so inside impl Default for Editor, Self { … } constructs an Editor. That is why main will be able to say Editor::default().

And the & in edit 2 means borrow: let the label read your text without taking it away. Write self.text without the & and you'd hand the String over permanently; the compiler stops you. Ownership is coming into focus.

Edit 3 is a real error, and finding it is the exercise Once Editor has a field, the bare name Editor is a type, not a value — so whatever main was handing to eframe is no longer a thing that exists. Run cargo check, read error[E0423], and fix it from what it tells you. Then run cargo fmt.

How you'll know

cargo run
→ "Hello, editor." under the heading. You can't type in it. It's a label.

Hint — the shape of the Default impl, and what E0423 wants

The Default implementation has the same grammar as the eframe::App one you typed in stage 2: impl Trait for Type, with the required function inside. This trait requires one function, called default, which takes nothing and returns Self.

The body is a struct literal: the type's name (or Self), braces, and each field set to a value — text: "…".to_owned(),. Note the trailing comma; Rust wants one on every field.

For E0423: you now have a way to make an Editor value that you did not have before. Use it where the bare type name currently sits.

The code — three edits, in order

First edit. An editor needs a buffer, so give Editor a field. Replace struct Editor; from stage 2 — don't add alongside it, or you define the same name twice:

editor/src/main.rstop of the file

use eframe::egui;

struct Editor;
struct Editor {
    text: String,
}

impl Default for Editor {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            text: "Hello, editor.\n".to_owned(),
        }
    }
}

Second edit — draw that text. One line, under the heading:

editor/src/main.rsin fn ui, under the heading

        egui::CentralPanel::default().show(ui, |ui| {
            ui.heading("editor");
            ui.label(&self.text);
        });

Third edit, elsewhere in the file. In main, Box::new(Editor) no longer works: Editor has a field now, so the bare name is a type, not a value. Miss this one and you get error[E0423]: expected value, found struct `Editor`.

editor/src/main.rsat the bottom of main

    eframe::run_native("editor", options, Box::new(|_cc| Ok(Box::new(Editor))))
    eframe::run_native(
        "editor",
        options,
        Box::new(|_cc| Ok(Box::new(Editor::default()))),
    )

It grew from one line to five only because ::default() pushed it past rustfmt's line width, so cargo fmt breaks the arguments out. Same call, wrapped.

Words you just met
field
A named piece of data inside a struct, reached with a dot: self.text.
owned
This value is yours; you decide when it dies. A String is owned.
borrowed
You have access to something somebody else owns, for a while. Written with &.
heap
Memory that can grow and shrink while the program runs, and whose size need not be known at compile time. A String's text lives there.
stack
Memory that comes and goes with function calls, fixed-size and very fast. The String value itself — a pointer, a length, a capacity — lives there.
string literal
Text in quotes in your source. Its type is &str, and it is baked into the binary, so it cannot grow.
&str vs String
Borrowed fixed text vs owned growable text. Nearly every Rust beginner's first hour of confusion lives in this row.
Self
Capital S: the type an impl block is about. Lowercase self: the value a method was called on. Different things.
associated function
A function on a type that does not take self, called as Type::name(). Editor::default() is one. Other languages call this a static method.
Default
A trait from the standard library meaning "there is a sensible starting value for this type". Implementing it is how Editor::default() came to exist.
struct literal
How you build a struct value: Self { text: … }. Every field must be given a value — Rust has no partially-built structs.
E0423
"Expected value, found struct." You used a type's name where a value was needed — the error you were sent to find in edit 3.

Make it editable — the stage that fails first

Write the wrong version on purpose, then let the compiler teach you the rule.

Understand &mut by getting it wrong, on purpose.

What to build

  1. A label can't be edited, so swap it for a text box: ui.add(egui::TextEdit::multiline(…)), replacing the ui.label(…) line. Pass it exactly what you passed the label — &self.text. Try the obvious thing; keep the & you already know.
  2. Run cargo check. It will not compile. Read the error, answer the question below it, then make the one-token fix.
  3. Once it compiles, make it look like a code editor: monospaced font, full width. Two more calls chained onto the TextEdit before it goes into ui.add — .font(egui::TextStyle::Monospace) and .desired_width(f32::INFINITY).

cargo check
— faster than cargo run, and it won't produce a binary. Use it whenever you're arguing with the compiler.

What the compiler will say

Roughly this, and the shape matters more than the wording:

error[E0308]: mismatched types
   --> src/main.rs:19:46
    |
 19 |             ui.add(egui::TextEdit::multiline(&self.text));
    |                    ------------------------- ^^^^^^^^^^ types differ in mutability
    |                    |
    |                    arguments to this function are incorrect
    |
    = note: expected mutable reference `&mut dyn TextBuffer`
                       found reference `&String`
Before reading on: types differ in mutability. What is the text box asking for that a label didn't need, and why?

A label only ever reads your text. A text box has to write into it — when you press a key, that character has to end up in your String. So it needs a stronger kind of access than & can give.

This is the heart of Rust. Every value has one owner, and access is granted through borrows, of which there are exactly two kinds:

BorrowWrittenHow many at onceWhat you may do
Shared & Any number Read only. Never modify.
Exclusive &mut Exactly one, ever Modify freely. Nobody else can even look while you hold it.

The rule underneath: many readers, or one writer — never both at once. That one rule is what lets Rust eliminate data races at compile time, and it's the rule you'll spend the next month arguing with. Now make the fix yourself — it is one token, in one place.

And when it compiles, work out why &mut self from stage 2 had to be there. You can only hand out &mut self.text if you hold exclusive access to self — a shared borrow can't be upgraded into an exclusive one. That token is a permission slip, and without it typing would be impossible.

Worth doing: change &mut self to &self in the ui signature and run cargo check again. Two errors, not one — the borrow error, and a complaint that your ui no longer matches the signature eframe::App requires. Two lessons in one mistake. Put it back after.

How you'll know

cargo run
→ Type in it. This is a text editor now, for a generous definition of "editor".

The code — the broken line, the fix, and the expansion

The version that fails, for comparison with yours:

editor/src/main.rsin fn ui, replacing the label

            ui.heading("editor");
            ui.label(&self.text);
            ui.add(egui::TextEdit::multiline(&self.text));

The fix — one token:

editor/src/main.rssame line, in fn ui

            ui.add(egui::TextEdit::multiline(&mut self.text));

Read it as: here is my buffer — you may write directly into it. A keypress pushes that character into your String. No copy, no synchronisation step, no reading the value back out afterwards.

And the expansion, monospaced and full width:

editor/src/main.rsin fn ui, expanding the TextEdit

            ui.add(
                egui::TextEdit::multiline(&mut self.text)
                    .font(egui::TextStyle::Monospace)
                    .desired_width(f32::INFINITY),
            );
Words you just met
ownership
Every value has exactly one owner, and is cleaned up when the owner goes out of scope. No garbage collector, no manual free.
shared borrow (&)
Read-only access. Any number at once.
exclusive borrow (&mut)
Read-and-write access. Exactly one at a time, and nobody else may even read meanwhile.
mutable (mut)
Changeable. Everything in Rust is immutable until you say otherwise — the opposite default from most languages.
data race
Two things touching the same data at once, one of them writing. The borrow rule makes this a compile error rather than a bug you hunt at 2am.
builder pattern
Each call returns the thing back so you can chain another: multiline(…).font(…).desired_width(…). egui is built on this.
f32
A 32-bit floating point number. f32::INFINITY here means "as wide as there is room for".
E0308
"Mismatched types" — the most common Rust error there is. The note: lines under it tell you what was expected and what arrived.

Prove there's only one source of truth

One line. Then the idea the whole lesson exists for.

A live byte count that you never wired up to anything.

What to build

  1. One more line, below the text box: a label showing how many bytes are in your buffer. You will need format! — a macro that builds a String from a template, where {} marks a slot — and .len(), which on a String counts bytes.

Deliberately do not wire it up to anything. No callback, no event, no update step. Write only the label, run it, and type into the box.

How you'll know

cargo run
→ a byte counter that moves as you type

Hint — the shape of the format! call

ui.label(…) again, but instead of a reference to a field you hand it the String that format! just built — that one is owned and brand new, so it needs no &.

The template is a string literal with a {} where the number goes, followed by a comma and the value to put there.

The code — one line

editor/src/main.rsin fn ui, below the TextEdit

                    .desired_width(f32::INFINITY),
            );
            ui.label(format!("{} bytes", self.text.len()));
This is the whole lesson Nothing connects that label to that text box. No event, no listener, no data binding, no onChange. The label is simply recomputed from self.text on the next frame — and a frame happens because you pressed a key.

This is immediate mode, and it's why we chose egui. In a retained mode toolkit (GTK, Qt, the DOM) you create a text box object, register a callback, and keep your data in sync with the widget's copy. Two sources of truth, with most GUI bugs living in the gap. The egui README puts it directly:

"In a retained GUI you create a button, add it to some UI and install some on-click handler (callback)… By contrast, in immediate mode you show the button and interact with it immediately, and you do so every frame."

"You don't have to worry about app state and GUI state being out-of-sync… because the GUI isn't storing any state — it is showing the latest state immediately."

— emilk/egui README

"Every frame" is the model you code against, not what actually happens. egui "only repaints when there is interaction (e.g. mouse movement) or an animation, so if your app is idle, no CPU is wasted" (README FAQ).

The bill comes due later Immediate mode redoes the full layout every frame, so per the same README, "the layout code needs to be quick… having a very large UI in a scroll area (with very long scrollback) can be slow." A promise that we fight this crate around lesson 6, when a 50,000-line file meets a naive redraw.
Words you just met
format!
A macro that builds a String from a template. {} is a slot; the values come after the comma.
frame
One pass of drawing the whole UI. Your ui function is a frame.
repaint
Running another frame. egui does one when something happens — a keypress, a mouse move — not sixty times a second regardless.
immediate mode
You describe the whole UI every frame from your own data. Widgets keep no state, so nothing can drift out of sync.
retained mode
The older model: you create widget objects that live on, and keep their contents in sync with your data by hand. GTK, Qt and the DOM all work this way.
callback
A function you hand to a toolkit to be called later, when something happens. The thing immediate mode lets you stop writing.
source of truth
The one place a fact actually lives. Here it is self.text, and nowhere else.
bytes vs characters
.len() counts bytes, not letters — é is two. Lesson 4 makes you care about the difference.

Where you ended up

Forty lines. Diff yours against it, and run cargo fmt — the community standard, no configuration, no debate.

The finished file — to diff against, once yours runs

editor/src/main.rs

use eframe::egui;

struct Editor {
    text: String,
}

impl Default for Editor {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            text: "Hello, editor.\n".to_owned(),
        }
    }
}

impl eframe::App for Editor {
    fn ui(&mut self, ui: &mut egui::Ui, _frame: &mut eframe::Frame) {
        egui::CentralPanel::default().show(ui, |ui| {
            ui.heading("editor");
            ui.add(
                egui::TextEdit::multiline(&mut self.text)
                    .font(egui::TextStyle::Monospace)
                    .desired_width(f32::INFINITY),
            );
            ui.label(format!("{} bytes", self.text.len()));
        });
    }
}

fn main() -> eframe::Result {
    let options = eframe::NativeOptions {
        viewport: egui::ViewportBuilder::default().with_inner_size([800.0, 600.0]),
        ..Default::default()
    };

    eframe::run_native(
        "editor",
        options,
        Box::new(|_cc| Ok(Box::new(Editor::default()))),
    )
}

Check yourself

Don't skip these. Recall builds far more durable memory than re-reading — and you need this in six months, in an interview. Each explanation links back to where the idea was taught; Back returns you here.

You type "fn" into the window. Between that frame and the next, where does that text physically live?

  • In the Editor struct's field
  • In the TextEdit widget's object
  • In the egui::Ui layout tree
  • In the eframe window's handle

Immediate-mode widgets are transient — that TextEdit is constructed and thrown away every single frame. Your struct is the only thing that survives between frames, which is exactly why nothing can fall out of sync. ↑ Review: one source of truth (stage 6)

Stage 4's ui.label(&self.text) compiled fine. Why did the same & fail for TextEdit?

  • A text box writes; a label only reads
  • Labels copy the string; text boxes borrow it
  • Text boxes need owned data, not borrowed
  • Labels take a str, text boxes a String

Exactly what E0308: types differ in mutability was telling you. A shared borrow grants read access; typing is a write, so TextEdit demands an exclusive &mut borrow instead. ↑ Review: the two kinds of borrow (stage 5)

What does impl eframe::App for Editor actually claim?

  • Editor provides every function that trait demands
  • Editor inherits the behaviour of a parent class
  • eframe::App gains a new method called Editor
  • Editor becomes a copy of the App type

Read impl X for Y as "Y keeps X's promises". It is a contract, not inheritance — there is no parent class anywhere, and the compiler checks every signature in the contract before it accepts the block. ↑ Review: trait, implement, signature (stage 2)

Your app sits open and untouched for a minute. Roughly how many times does ui run?

  • Almost none — input drives repaints
  • About 3,600 — sixty frames per second
  • Exactly one — the initial layout pass
  • Thousands — capped by the display's refresh

"Every frame" is the mental model you code against, but egui only repaints on interaction or animation, so an idle app costs no CPU. You get immediate mode's simplicity without the battery drain you'd expect. ↑ Review: when egui actually repaints (stage 6)

Primary source: The Rust Programming Language, Chapter 4 — Understanding Ownership (Brown University interactive edition). Read 4.1 and 4.2; 4.3 can wait.

Use this edition, not the official one. Same book, plus inline quizzes you retry to mastery and diagrams that animate memory as the code runs. Its ownership chapter was rewritten around research into what learners actually get wrong. Stage 5 gave you the rule; chapter 4 gives you the reasons.
